name: Naloxone (Narcan)
summary: Fast opioid antidote that can reverse an overdose in minutes. It’s a rescue med, not a treatment plan—effects can wear off before the opioid does, so emergency care is still mandatory.
description: Naloxone is an opioid blocker used to reverse opioid overdose (slow or stopped breathing, extreme sleepiness, unresponsiveness). It can work within 2 to 5 minutes (IV/IM) or within minutes intranasally, but it doesn’t last long—people can slip back into overdose when it wears off. It can also trigger sudden, intense opioid withdrawal (agitation, vomiting, sweating, pain). Give naloxone, call 911, and stay with the person until help arrives.
patient_summary: Naloxone is an opioid blocker used to reverse opioid overdose (slow or stopped breathing, extreme sleepiness, unresponsiveness). It can work fast, but it doesn’t last long—people can slip back into overdose when it wears off. It can also trigger sudden, intense opioid withdrawal (agitation, vomiting, sweating, pain). Give naloxone, call 911, and stay with the person until help arrives.

metadata.prescription_status: Varies by product (some OTC intranasal products; others prescription)

primary_indications: Emergency treatment of known or suspected opioid overdose (respiratory and/or CNS depression)
Complete or partial reversal of opioid-induced respiratory depression
Diagnostic use in suspected acute opioid overdose (clinical setting)

linked_conditions.context: Naloxone is a first-line rescue medication when opioid overdose is suspected—especially when breathing is slow, shallow, or absent. It buys time, but it does not replace emergency medical care.
Naloxone is a harm-reduction tool. Many clinical guidelines recommend making naloxone available to people at risk for overdose and to family/friends likely to witness one.

Naloxone only reverses opioid-related respiratory depression. If there is no meaningful response after adequate dosing, clinicians should urgently consider other causes (non-opioid sedatives, medical illness, hypoglycemia, stroke, etc.).

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to naloxone or any component of the formulation

efficacy_response.metric: Return of adequate breathing after administration
efficacy_response.patient_text: Naloxone can rapidly reverse opioid-related slowed or stopped breathing. If the person doesn’t improve after repeated doses, it’s a major red flag that something else may be going on—or the opioid exposure is unusually potent/long-acting—so emergency care is non-negotiable.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: AHA Opioid-Associated Emergency Guidance; FDA labeling

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Intranasal, IM, and SUBQ absorption can be delayed or variable (especially with poor perfusion); IV provides the fastest, most predictable effect.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Intranasal bioavailability is lower than IV; product-specific performance varies by formulation and concentration.
pharmacokinetics.onset: IV ~2 minutes; IM/SUBQ ~2 to 5 minutes; intranasal ~3 to 17 minutes (varies by product and situation).
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Intranasal and IM peak concentrations typically occur within ~15 to 30 minutes depending on product.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Adults: ~0.5 to 1.5 hours (IM/IV/SUBQ); intranasal ~1.1 to 2 hours (product-dependent).
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: ~30 to 120 minutes depending on route and dose; often shorter than the opioid involved, so repeat dosing and observation are commonly required.
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: Relatively weak (binds to albumin and other plasma constituents).

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Naloxone is a rescue medication for opioid overdose. Think of it like a fire extinguisher: it can save a life in the moment, but you still need the fire department. It’s used when opioids are causing dangerous sleepiness or slowed/stopped breathing.
items: {link:condition:opioid-overdose:Opioid overdose}: Emergency reversal of opioid-related respiratory depression and unresponsiveness
Opioid toxicity in medical settings: Full or partial reversal when opioids are suppressing breathing
Harm reduction: Carried by people at risk for overdose and by family/friends who might witness an overdose
off_label: {link:condition:opioid-use-disorder:Opioid use disorder (naloxone challenge)}: Used in supervised settings to confirm opioid-free status before starting certain medications (specialist use)
Clonidine toxicity: Limited data; specialist/poison control guidance recommended

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Naloxone isn’t a “feel better” med—it's a rescue reversal. When it works, the experience can be intense and abrupt:

quotes: It was like someone hit the reset button—one second out, the next second I was awake.
I went from barely there to fully alert way too fast.
It felt abrupt and jarring, like being yanked back into my body.

items.category: Withdrawal whiplash (common if someone is opioid-dependent)
quotes: Instant misery—sweats, nausea, shaking, and panic all at once.
I felt furious and sick at the same time. Like my skin was crawling.
My body hurt everywhere, and I couldn’t sit still.
items.note: This is naloxone doing its job: it knocks opioids off receptors fast. That can trigger acute withdrawal.

quotes: I woke up confused and pissed off. I didn’t know what happened.
I felt cornered and panicky when I came to.
It took a minute to realize people were trying to help me.
items.note: After reversal, some people are disoriented or agitated. Safety matters—step back and let EMS handle it if possible.

quotes: I felt better, then later I started nodding again.
It worked… and then it didn’t. That second crash was scary.
I thought I was fine, but my breathing got bad again.
items.note: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does. That’s why calling 911 and monitoring is essential.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Naloxone can work fast—sometimes within minutes—but the clock matters. Its effects often fade in 30 to 120 minutes, and many opioids last longer.
key_points: IV: ~2 minutes to start working (fastest, most predictable in medical settings)
IM/SUBQ: ~2 to 5 minutes to start working
Intranasal: roughly ~3 to 17 minutes depending on product, dose, and situation
Duration: ~30 to 120 minutes (often shorter than the opioid involved), so repeat dosing and observation are common
If breathing worsens again after initial improvement, give another dose and keep emergency help coming

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Naloxone is highly effective at reversing opioid effects when opioids are the reason a person’s breathing is dangerously slowed or stopped. The exact response depends on the opioid (short vs long acting), potency (including fentanyl analogs), the dose taken, and how quickly help arrives. If there’s no meaningful response after repeated dosing, clinicians should urgently consider other causes of respiratory depression.
sections.clinical_details: Guidelines for opioid-associated emergencies recommend naloxone when opioid poisoning is suspected, alongside immediate activation of emergency response and airway/breathing support. For cardiac arrest, CPR and AED take priority, with naloxone considered as part of the response when opioid poisoning is suspected.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Naloxone is not a substitute for emergency care. Call 911 after the first dose—even if the person wakes up.
other: Recurrence risk: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid does. Breathing problems can return and can be fatal without monitoring.
Acute opioid withdrawal: Can be sudden and severe (vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, agitation, pain, fast heart rate, high blood pressure).
Agitation/combativeness: Some people wake up confused, frightened, and reactive—keep safety in mind.
Cardiovascular risk: Abrupt reversal can stress the body; use caution in people with cardiovascular disease (rare serious events reported).
Partial agonists: Overdoses involving buprenorphine or mixed agonist/antagonists may respond incompletely and may require repeated dosing plus ventilatory support.
patient_counseling: Call 911 immediately after the first naloxone dose. Don’t “wait and see.”
If there’s no response, repeat dosing per product directions while continuing rescue breathing/CPR if needed.
Stay with the person. Put them on their side (recovery position) once they’re breathing on their own.
Expect withdrawal symptoms if the person is opioid-dependent. This can look like panic, anger, vomiting, sweating, diarrhea, shaking, and severe body aches.
Even if they wake up and feel okay, they can slip back into overdose when naloxone wears off—this is the big danger.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most side effects are really “opioid withdrawal symptoms” caused by rapid reversal. In overdose rescue, the benefit is lifesaving—even if the wake-up is rough.
plain_language_list: Sudden opioid withdrawal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, shaking, body aches, anxiety, irritability)
Agitation, confusion, or combativeness after waking up
Changes in blood pressure or heart rate (can swing up or down)
Nasal discomfort (intranasal products): runny nose, congestion, irritation

common.incidence: Frequency varies (more likely in opioid-dependent patients and with higher doses)
common.patient_note: This can feel brutal: sweating, shaking, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, gooseflesh, yawning, agitation, anxiety, and intense body pain. It’s not “an allergy”—it’s the opioid being kicked off receptors fast.
Some people wake up disoriented and reactive. This is common enough that responders plan for it. Safety first.

common.symptom: Blood pressure and heart rate changes
common.patient_note: Withdrawal can spike heart rate and blood pressure. In medically fragile patients, clinicians monitor closely.
Runny nose, congestion, sneezing, nasal discomfort can happen. In an overdose rescue, this is background noise compared to restoring breathing.

serious: Recurrent respiratory depression after initial improvement (medical emergency): give another dose and get emergency help
Pulmonary edema (rare but reported): severe shortness of breath, frothy sputum, low oxygen—medical emergency
Severe agitation or violence after reversal (safety risk)
Seizures (rare; reported particularly in neonates and in specific clinical contexts)
Serious cardiovascular instability (rare): arrhythmias and other events reported after abrupt reversal in high-risk patients

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Naloxone’s “interaction” is the point: it blocks opioids. That’s lifesaving in overdose, but it can also reverse pain control and trigger withdrawal.

items.with: Opioids (any opioid agonist, including prescription opioids, heroin, fentanyl)
items.risk: Reverses opioid effects, including pain relief; may trigger acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent people.
items.action: In overdose, give naloxone and call 911. In medical settings (post-op, chronic pain), clinicians often titrate small IV doses to restore breathing without fully wiping out analgesia.

items.with: Buprenorphine and mixed agonist/antagonists (e.g., buprenorphine, pentazocine)
items.risk: Reversal may be incomplete and may require repeated doses; ventilatory support may still be necessary.
items.action: Give naloxone per protocol, repeat as needed, and prioritize airway/ventilation. Don’t assume “it didn’t work” means “not an overdose.”

items.with: Non-opioid sedatives (benzodiazepines, alcohol, sedating antihistamines, etc.)
items.risk: Naloxone does not reverse non-opioid sedation; overdose may be mixed.
items.action: If there’s limited response to naloxone, treat as a medical emergency and continue supportive care (breathing support, EMS).

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
key_points: Naloxone is used as rescue or short-term reversal, not as a daily medication that requires tapering.
The main safety issue is not “tapering”—it’s monitoring for recurrence of overdose when naloxone wears off.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Naloxone dosing is about getting breathing back, fast, while avoiding unnecessary full-on withdrawal when possible (especially in clinical settings). In the community, follow the product directions and keep repeating doses until emergency help takes over.

adult.overdose_iv_initial: 0.04 to 2 mg IV (preferred); repeat with escalating doses every 2 to 3 minutes as needed based on breathing/response. If severe toxicity (respiratory or cardiorespiratory arrest), starting closer to the higher end may be appropriate.
adult.overdose_iv_max_consider_other_causes: If no response after a cumulative 10 mg, urgently consider non-opioid causes of respiratory depression; some high-potency opioid exposures may still require larger total doses based on clinical response.
adult.overdose_iv_redose_window: After reversal, repeat dosing may be needed again at longer intervals (about every 20 to 60 minutes) depending on the opioid’s duration.
adult.overdose_infusion_off_label: For long-acting opioids (e.g., methadone), extended-release exposures, or delayed absorption: start continuous IV infusion at 2/3 of the initial effective bolus per hour (usual range ~0.25 to 6.25 mg/hour), then titrate to maintain ventilation and minimize withdrawal.
adult.overdose_im_subq_initial: 0.04 to 2 mg IM or SUBQ; repeat with escalating doses every 2 to 3 minutes as needed when IV is not available.
adult.overdose_intranasal: 3 mg, 4 mg, or 8 mg intranasal (one device in one nostril); repeat with a new device every 2 to 3 minutes in alternating nostrils if there is no response or if breathing worsens again after initial improvement.
adult.therapeutic_opioid_partial_reversal_acut: IV 0.05 to 0.2 mg every 2 to 3 minutes until adequate ventilation/alertness without fully reversing pain control; repeat doses may be needed within 1 to 2 hours depending on opioid used.
adult.therapeutic_opioid_partial_reversal_chro: IV 0.02 to 0.08 mg slow bolus every 30 to 120 seconds until improvement; if no response after cumulative 1 mg, consider other causes. For long-acting opioids, consider infusion at 2/3 of the effective bolus per hour (or ~0.2 mg/hour) and titrate.
adult.naloxone_challenge_off_label: IV: 0.2 mg once; if withdrawal signs appear within ~30 seconds, stop and treat symptoms; if not, give 0.6 mg and observe ~20 minutes. Alternative routes: IM 0.4 to 0.8 mg once or SUBQ 0.8 mg once with observation per protocol (specialist-supervised).

sections.simple_explanation: Naloxone is short-acting. It can restart breathing, but it can also wear off while the opioid is still active—so people can go back into overdose. That’s why repeat doses and emergency care are built into every naloxone plan.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Naloxone can be used in pregnancy when it’s needed to save a life. Yes, it can trigger withdrawal, but untreated overdose is worse. In older adults and medically fragile patients, clinicians still use it—just with close monitoring because abrupt reversal can stress the cardiovascular system.
sections.pregnancy: Naloxone crosses the placenta and can trigger withdrawal in the fetus as well as the mother, but guidelines emphasize it should not be withheld in maternal overdose because maternal survival is the priority. In clinical settings, clinicians may start at the low end and titrate to restore breathing while minimizing abrupt withdrawal when feasible.
sections.lactation: It’s not clearly known how much naloxone enters breast milk, and oral absorption is minimal. In real-world practice, naloxone use for overdose rescue is not a reason to withhold lifesaving care. If ongoing treatment decisions are needed, clinicians weigh infant exposure risk against benefits of breastfeeding and maternal health.
sections.pediatrics: Used for pediatric opioid overdose with weight-based dosing in younger children and fixed dosing in older children/adolescents in many emergency protocols. IM and intranasal administration may be delayed or erratic in low-perfusion states, so careful monitoring and repeat dosing are often required.
sections.geriatrics: Dose is generally the same as in younger adults, but older adults may have more cardiovascular vulnerability and may be more sensitive to abrupt physiologic stress; monitor closely after reversal.
sections.hepatic: No specific manufacturer dose adjustment guidance. Because metabolism is hepatic, clinicians monitor response and adverse effects in significant liver disease, especially if continuous infusion is used.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is generally needed, but prolonged effects have been reported in advanced kidney impairment during continuous infusion; monitor for extended opioid antagonism and recurrence of symptoms.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Breathing and oxygenation: respiratory rate, effort, oxygen saturation; be ready for repeat dosing and ventilatory support
Level of consciousness and airway protection: improvement after dosing, aspiration risk if vomiting occurs
Recurrence: watch for return of sedation or slowed breathing as naloxone wears off (especially with long-acting opioids or large exposures)
Vital signs: heart rate, blood pressure, temperature (withdrawal can drive spikes; abrupt reversal can stress high-risk patients)
Withdrawal symptoms: agitation, sweating, yawning, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, muscle aches, tremor
Pain control (in therapeutic opioid settings): titrate to restore ventilation without unnecessarily eliminating analgesia
Need for escalation: if minimal response after adequate dosing, consider mixed overdose or non-opioid causes and escalate care immediately

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Naloxone comes in nasal sprays and injections. The best product is the one you can actually access and use correctly in an emergency.
items: Intranasal spray: 3 mg/0.1 mL (e.g., RiVive), single-use device
Intranasal spray: 4 mg/0.1 mL (e.g., Narcan and other 4 mg products), single-use device
Intranasal spray: 8 mg/0.1 mL (e.g., Kloxxado), single-use device
Injection solution: 0.4 mg/mL (vials/ampules/prefilled syringes; clinical use and some community programs)
Injection solution: higher-concentration products exist for specific delivery systems (product-dependent)
Prefilled syringe: 5 mg/0.5 mL (e.g., Zimhi), IM/SUBQ
Auto-injector: 10 mg/0.4 mL (specialized use cases; device-guided administration)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist. It competes with opioids and kicks them off opioid receptors (especially the mu receptor). When opioids are suppressing breathing, naloxone can reverse that suppression—fast.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Naloxone is harm reduction, period. If opioids are in the picture—prescribed or illicit—naloxone belongs in the safety plan. For people with opioid use disorder, it’s standard to educate patients and their support network on overdose recognition, naloxone administration, and immediate activation of emergency response. In medical settings, clinicians often titrate smaller doses when the goal is partial reversal (restore breathing without fully reversing analgesia).

seo.title: Naloxone (Narcan): How It Reverses Opioid Overdose, Dosing, and What to Do Next
seo.description: Naloxone (Narcan) is a fast opioid antidote that can reverse overdose in minutes. Learn dosing by route (nasal, IM, IV), how long it lasts, withdrawal effects, repeat dosing, and why calling 911 is mandatory.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Naloxone is a rescue medication that reverses opioid overdose. It’s used when opioids are causing dangerous sleepiness or slow/stopped breathing. It’s not a substitute for medical care—after the first dose, emergency help still has to happen.

Yes, it can. But fentanyl and other high-potency opioids may require repeat doses. The rule is simple: give naloxone, call 911, and keep dosing per directions if breathing doesn’t improve or worsens again.

In medical settings, IV naloxone can start working in about 2 minutes. IM/SUBQ is often 2 to 5 minutes. Intranasal can be a bit slower and varies by product and situation—still fast enough to be lifesaving.

Usually about 30 to 120 minutes depending on the route and dose. Many opioids last longer, which is why people can slip back into overdose after initially waking up. That’s the big danger—monitoring and emergency care are essential.

faqs.q: Can naloxone hurt someone if it wasn’t an opioid overdose?
faqs.a: Naloxone won’t reverse non-opioid sedation (like benzos or alcohol), and it’s generally considered safe—but if opioids aren’t the cause, the person still needs emergency evaluation because something serious is happening. In opioid-dependent people, naloxone can trigger sudden withdrawal that feels awful, but the alternative (untreated overdose) can be fatal.

faqs.q: Why does someone get angry or sick after Narcan?
faqs.a: Because naloxone can trigger instant opioid withdrawal. That can look like agitation, panic, sweating, shaking, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, and severe body aches. It’s intense, but it’s a sign opioids were on the receptors and naloxone displaced them.

faqs.q: What should I do after giving naloxone?
faqs.a: Call 911 immediately after the first dose. Keep watching breathing and responsiveness. If there’s no improvement—or if they improve and then get worse again—give another dose per product directions. Put them on their side (recovery position) once breathing returns. Stay with them until EMS arrives.

faqs.q: Does naloxone reverse benzodiazepines or alcohol?
faqs.a: No. Naloxone only blocks opioids. If someone overdosed on benzos or alcohol (or it’s a mixed overdose), naloxone may do little or nothing—support breathing and get emergency help immediately.

faqs.q: Can naloxone work with buprenorphine overdose?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but reversal may be incomplete and may require repeated dosing plus ventilatory support. Buprenorphine binds tightly and lasts a long time, so airway/breathing support is critical while EMS takes over.

If a pregnant person is overdosing, naloxone should not be withheld. Yes, it can trigger withdrawal (including fetal stress), but untreated overdose is life-threatening. The priority is saving the mother’s life and getting emergency care.

faqs.q: Should people on opioids have naloxone at home?
faqs.a: Often, yes—especially if there are overdose risk factors (higher doses, combining opioids with other sedatives, history of overdose or substance use disorder). Many guidelines encourage offering naloxone not only to patients but also to family members or caregivers who might be present in an emergency.
